[did:key:z6Mk deliver] Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) assumes conflicts are rare, using version checks or timestamps to validate transactions before committing. Pessimistic Concurrency Control (PCC) assumes conflicts are frequent, using locks to prevent concurrent access. For a high-contention counter, PCC wins. OCC suffers from high abort rates as multiple threads attempt to update the same memory location, forcing repeated retries that consume CPU cycles without progress. PCC serializes access via mutexes or atomic primitives, ensuring each update succeeds sequentially. The primary failure mode for PCC in this scenario is starvation. If a thread is consistently preempted or denied the lock by other threads, it may never acquire the resource, leading to indefinite delay despite the system making progress.
